title: Ghost-Student Fraud Defense for Community Colleges
one_liner: Enrollment-fraud screening built into admissions and financial-aid workflows that separates real applicants from bot-driven ghost students before aid disburses.
customer: Community-college districts' admissions, financial-aid and IT-security offices, plus state college systems. There are about 1,000 community colleges in the US.
problem: Fraud rings use stolen or synthetic identities, and increasingly AI-completed coursework, to enroll and collect federal and state aid. California community colleges have reported large shares of applications as fraudulent and tens of millions of dollars lost. Regulators have tightened identity-verification requirements for aid recipients. Staff are overwhelmed by manual reviews, and consumer IDV tools do not fit education workflows.
solution: Integrate with student information and learning management systems. Risk-score at application, enrollment and first-week activity using LMS login patterns, IP and ASN reuse, device farms, writing similarity and disbursement-account reuse. Send only high-risk cases to paid ID verification, place aid holds, produce OIG-ready reports, and give auditors a dashboard.
why_now: The 2025-26 ghost-student wave hit colleges as AI agents got good enough to attend and submit work, and aid-verification rules tightened. State funding for fraud response exists.
revenue_model: $25-100K per district per year, or $0.10-0.50 per application screened.
non_obvious_insight: The budget owner is financial-aid compliance, driven by audit findings and risk to aid eligibility, not IT. The best signals (LMS behavior) exist only after enrollment, so this is behavioral IDV that consumer vendors cannot copy.
first_30_days: Pilot with 2 colleges. Retro-score one semester of application logs to show dollars at risk, pitch through financial-aid and CIO associations, and price at $2K per month.

title: GPS Spoofing Alarm Using LEO Signals
one_liner: A passive receiver that listens to Starlink, OneWeb and Iridium-style signals and flags when GPS disagrees.
customer: Shipping companies and port authorities in jammed regions (Baltic, Persian Gulf, Red Sea), aviation operators, telecom timing operators, drone fleets, and hull and P&I insurers.
problem: GNSS jamming and spoofing have spread across shipping and aviation (prior knowledge, 2024-25). Most detection depends on GNSS itself or expensive inertial systems. Operators and insurers want independent evidence of position integrity.
solution: A small software-defined receiver that measures Doppler and timing from LEO communication signals of opportunity and, using public orbit data, checks position and time consistency. First product is an integrity alarm, not a navigator. Later add tens-of-meters holdover navigation.
why_now: There are about 10,000 Starlinks plus other constellations, so signals of opportunity are abundant. Academic demonstrations of positioning from them have matured. Jamming has moved from a defense concern to a commercial one.
revenue_model: $2-5k per unit plus $100 per month cloud analytics. Insurer-funded fleet programs. Government pilots.
non_obvious_insight: You do not need to navigate better than GPS to be valuable, only to disagree with it reliably. Integrity is a cheaper, faster product than replacement navigation.
first_30_days: Build a lab proof of concept using a Ku-band LNB and an SDR. Recruit two Baltic or Gulf ship managers or port operators for field trials. Approach one marine insurer about premium credits for verified integrity.

title: Jobsite Translator That Teaches the Trade
one_liner: Live English-Spanish translation for construction crews that also logs each worker's vocabulary and safety instructions, turning toolbox talks into comprehension-verified training and a path to licensure.
customer: Mid-size specialty contractors (electrical, drywall, framing, roofing, concrete) with mixed-language crews, their safety directors, and union or association training funds.
problem: OSHA expects training delivered in a language and vocabulary workers understand. Language gaps cause incidents and keep capable helpers from advancing to licensed journeyman. Supervisors cannot verify comprehension, and ESL classes do not teach jobsite vocabulary.
solution: A phone and earbud app: real-time two-way translation with trade-specific glossaries, personalized micro-lessons built from each worker's actual jobsite phrases, comprehension checks after toolbox talks with signed training records, and an upskilling track toward licensing-exam vocabulary.
why_now: Consumer earbuds with live translation shipped in late 2025 and LLM translation now handles jargon with supplied glossaries. Labor shortages make retaining and upskilling existing crews more valuable.
revenue_model: $15-25 per worker per month paid by contractors, training-fund reimbursement, and a safety-compliance bundle.
non_obvious_insight: Translation removes the barrier in the moment, but the durable value is converting translated moments into a personalized curriculum and compliance record. The trade workforce is a captive, unserved learning audience, and safety compliance is an existing budget line.
first_30_days: Pilot with 2 contractors that have largely Spanish-speaking crews. Use the app in the weekly toolbox talk, then hand the safety director a comprehension-verification report. Charge $20 per worker and test on noisy sites early.

title: Rails Weather: Live Nigerian Payment Reliability Index
one_liner: An independent, always-on measurement of which bank-to-bank transfers are actually working right now, sold as an API and SLA evidence.
customer: Payment service providers, aggregators and mid-size fintechs that route transfers; large merchants and marketplaces; fintech partnership desks that need evidence in disputes with sponsor banks. Consumers get a free status page.
problem: Every Nigerian fintech founder knows transfer success varies by bank pair and hour. It drops at month-end salary rushes, on Friday evenings, and during weekend core-banking upgrades. Worst of all is the 'pending' or 'successful but not credited' limbo. Nobody publishes independent data, bank status pages are unreliable, and fintechs keep private dashboards. Users cope by keeping 3-5 accounts and switching to whichever works, and merchants insist on POS because they distrust transfers. Small fintechs cannot prove to sponsor banks or regulators where the failures originate.
solution: Run automated, staggered probe transfers between the team's own accounts across the top 10-15 banks and fintechs, measuring success rate, time-to-credit and the pending-then-resolve rate. Only the transfer fee is lost, since the money returns to a team account. Publish a free public status page for reach. Sell a routing-intelligence API (best rail or account right now, expected delay), monthly SLA-evidence reports, and alerts. Later, add a privacy-safe data co-op in which fintechs contribute anonymised outcome counts in exchange for deeper, real-time bank-pair data.
why_now: CBN moved 2026 into an enforcement year, with open banking, APP-fraud and failed-transaction rules all coming due together. Fintechs now have to show measured reliability, not just assert it. POS and transfer volume has exploded (5.9 million active POS terminals; N10.5 trillion of POS transactions in Q1 2025 alone). Cheap serverless probing and LLM-written incident summaries make a two-person team viable.
revenue_model: API subscription tiers of about N250k to N3m per month depending on volume. Enterprise SLA and dispute-evidence reports at N1-5m per report. A data-co-op membership fee. A sponsored 'Nigeria Payments Index' report for banks and media.
non_obvious_insight: The key metric is time-to-credit and the size of the ambiguous-pending bucket, not success rate. Banks report 'success' at the API level while customers wait hours. Independent measurement is also the only neutral evidence in the fight between sponsor banks and fintechs over who caused a failure, and neither side can publish it themselves.
first_30_days: Open business accounts at 8-10 institutions. Write a probe scheduler that costs roughly N3m per month at a 15-minute cadence across about 100 pairs. Publish a public dashboard and a weekly 'worst bank pairs' thread that the fintech community shares. Offer 5 fintech CTOs a free 60-day API trial in return for feedback and sample failure logs. Convert the first 2-3 to paid once their own incident data lines up with the index.

title: Dry-Hole Atlas for Hydrogen, Helium, Geothermal
one_liner: Re-read a century of scanned well logs and gas analyses, once treated as junk, to find natural hydrogen, helium and hot rock, and sell the resulting atlas to exploration companies by area of interest.
customer: Junior exploration companies and VC-backed developers in natural hydrogen, helium and geothermal (and lithium-brine plays), plus land and mineral-lease advisors who need leads. They pay for subscriptions and area-of-interest data packs.
problem: The US has millions of drilled wells. Old records include gas analyses, bottom-hole temperatures, water chemistry and mud-log shows, mostly recorded as incidental noise by oil and gas operators. They sit as scanned TIFFs and PDFs at state geological surveys and core repositories. New subsurface commodities need exactly this once-discarded information. Oil-and-gas data vendors index hydrocarbon fields, not hydrogen, helium or heat, and small explorers cannot afford to hire teams to dig through archives across 30 state surveys.
solution: A scan-to-structured-data pipeline across public state survey archives. Extract gas composition (hydrogen, helium, nitrogen), bottom-hole temperature and depth, and brine chemistry. Geolocate every record, correct for known temperature-log biases, and publish a queryable map atlas with prospectivity layers per township or section. Sell by area of interest. Offer custom queries such as 'every well within 20 miles of this substation with more than 0.3% helium and temperature above 150 C at 3 km'.
why_now: AI data centers are driving huge demand for clean firm power, and geothermal developers are raising large rounds and signing hyperscaler offtakes. Natural hydrogen exploration has attracted venture money and government attention. Helium supply has been unstable and prices volatile. Vision-language models now extract tables from old scans cheaply, and state surveys are increasingly open to releasing data.
revenue_model: Subscriptions of 15-50k USD per year per company for a basin or state atlas, area-of-interest packs of 5-25k USD, custom data services, and, later, small overriding royalties or success fees on leases won using the data.
non_obvious_insight: The value of data flips when the target commodity changes. A well that reported 'gas contains 40% hydrogen' in 1935 was a dud then, and it is a discovery lead today. Every incumbent data vendor is organized around the old commodity, so nobody re-reads the archive for byproducts. The archives are public and low-margin for the state agencies that hold them, so the moat is the extraction pipeline, cleaning and geological calibration, not data access.
first_30_days: Pick one state survey with well-documented public scans and gas-analysis reports and one target commodity (helium or hydrogen shows are the easiest to demo). Build a proof-of-concept map for one basin using a few thousand well records. Cold-email about 30 junior exploration companies and geothermal developers with the map and one concrete lead they can check. Sell 3-5 area-of-interest packs at around 5k USD each, and ask for pre-payment for the next state.

title: Philanthropic First-Loss Pool for Vet Care Loans
one_liner: Use foundation money as a loan guarantee instead of a grant, so each philanthropic dollar backs many dollars of low-APR vet credit that recycles as owners repay.
customer: Credit unions and CDFIs (lenders), private foundations (guarantee capital via program-related investments), and clinics (merchant side). End borrowers are middle-income owners who decline care.
problem: The briefing says 13% of euthanasias are attributed to inability to pay, and half of owners would be stressed by a bill of $1,000 or less. Options today are deferred-interest cards with 30%-plus APRs after the promo period, or subprime fintech loans. New philanthropy (Duffield $250M over 5 years; first grants are 250 x $10K) can't fund per-case care one grant at a time.
solution: A 'Care Guarantee Pool': a foundation funds a first-loss reserve (say 10-15% of a loan portfolio). A partner credit union or CDFI originates fixed-rate installment loans of $500-$5,000 at the clinic front desk, and the clinic is paid in about 48 hours. The vet's treatment plan is attached as collateral evidence to limit fraud, with an option to assign insurance proceeds. We run the program: clinic onboarding, application flow, servicing data and outcome reporting ('pets treated instead of euthanized').
why_now: The Duffield Foundation committed $250M on 2026-09-17, on top of PetSmart Charities' $100M pledge. Funders are looking for leverage and measurable outcomes. Embedded-lending rails (bank-as-a-service, instant payouts) make a lender-agnostic origination flow cheap to build.
revenue_model: 1-2% annual program-management fee on guaranteed balances (paid by the foundation), 2-3% origination fee from clinics, and a servicing share from the lender. Later, licensing of performance data.
non_obvious_insight: Philanthropy frames access as a subsidy problem. For the many owners who would repay an $1,800 bill over 12 months at 8% but face 30% APR or a deferred-interest trap, it is a cost-of-capital problem. A guarantee makes a one-shot grant a revolving fund, and it gives funders the proof they crave.
first_30_days: Get an LOI from one credit union or CDFI. Recruit 3 affordable-care clinics in one metro. Pitch a local community foundation and PetSmart Charities for a $250K pilot reserve (roughly $2M of loans). Use the lender's existing loan-origination software plus a simple clinic link. Model expected loss from 12-month payment-plan data at the clinics.

title: Programmable Lockbox for GPU and Robot Collateral
one_liner: Tri-party custody software and hardware that lets lenders verify, and if needed take over, financed GPU clusters and robot fleets sitting in someone else's building.
customer: Specialty and private-credit lenders and equipment lessors financing GPU clouds and robots-as-a-service. Borrowers such as neoclouds and robot operators pay to lower their borrowing spread, and colo operators act as a channel.
problem: More than $20B of loans are now secured by GPUs, and H100-class rental rates fell from about $7-10 per hour in early 2024 to $2-4 by late 2025, so lenders must know whether machines exist, are powered and utilised, and are not double-pledged. Monitoring today is a spreadsheet plus quarterly audits. The bigger trapdoors are the colo landlord's lien for unpaid power or rent and who physically or remotely controls the hardware on default.
solution: (1) A continuous collateral-health feed: hardware serials and attestation (TPM or GPU attestation where available), BMC and out-of-band data, power-meter readings, latency-based geolocation, and periodic photo audits by colo remote hands. (2) Escrowed step-in credentials for BMC and fleet consoles, plus a tri-party lockbox agreement with the colo covering access and lien waivers, with API-triggered 'freeze' and 'transfer to lender' modes. (3) Standard borrowing-base reports.
why_now: GPU-collateralised private credit scaled from almost nothing to over $20B in about two years, with loans maturing 2026-2028 among a small, correlated lender group. Banks avoid the fast-depreciating collateral, leaving private credit to fill the gap. Utilisation and location risk is now board-level for lenders. Robot-as-a-service leasing needs the same control layer.
revenue_model: $15-40 per GPU or robot per month paid by the borrower, or 10-25 bps on outstanding facility size, plus a $25k onboarding fee per facility and colo referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: Lender losses come from control failures such as liens, access and double-pledging, not from chips vanishing. Contracts plus access-control APIs solve most of it. The borrower is the real buyer, because a 50-100 bps lower spread beats the fee, so sell it to the neocloud CFO as a rate reduction.
first_30_days: Speak with 15 specialty lenders and equipment-finance boutiques and 10 GPU-cloud CFOs. Sell a manual 'collateral control audit' at $15-30k for two facilities. Draft the tri-party lockbox template with a finance lawyer, then productise the attestation feed.

title: Landing Fund: Sweden's Layoff Council for US Employers
one_liner: Employers pay about 0.3% of payroll into a pooled transition fund that gives every laid-off employee case management, retraining money and bridge pay, so companies can restructure without severance drama.
customer: CFOs and CHROs at 200-3,000-employee US companies (software, fintech, insurance, BPO, media) that are restructuring around AI or expect to. Reached through PEOs, HR brokers and benefits consultants.
problem: US severance is ad hoc (about 12-14 weeks for white-collar staff) and outplacement is usually a webinar. Leaders delay or botch layoffs because there is no humane, pre-agreed answer to 'what happens to the people we cut.' One tracker counts roughly 205,000 AI-attributed US layoffs through August 2026, concentrated in entry-level and back-office roles.
solution: A US version of Sweden's Trygghetsrådet (TRR). Employers join a pool at a set percentage of payroll. When someone is laid off they get a named case manager, retraining vouchers, a 2-4 month bridge-pay top-up, and a COBRA/health bridge subsidy, with providers paid partly on outcomes. Employers get a standard offboarding playbook, smaller bespoke severance, and less litigation and survivor-morale damage. Launch as prepaid 'transition credits' (no insurance license needed) and graduate to a captive or reinsured product.
why_now: AI became the top stated reason for corporate job cuts in the spring of 2026, entry-level white-collar hiring has collapsed, and executives are being publicly punished for how they lay people off. In Sweden the model covers 30,000+ companies and about 700,000 employees on 0.3% of payroll, and roughly 9 in 10 active clients found work, study or self-employment within seven months (2019 figures).
revenue_model: Per-employee-per-month or a percentage of payroll (0.2-0.4%). Unspent reserves fund the next cohort, with margin on training-partner rev share and, later, insurance float.
non_obvious_insight: Sweden's system works because employers fund it collectively, so no single firm carries the full cost of a big layoff, and that pooling turns a dreaded cost into a predictable premium. The buyer's real pain is decision speed and reputation, not the money. A ready-made, respected answer to 'what about the people' lets an executive act faster and more humanely, which is why the product can sell before any regulator asks for it.
first_30_days: Build a 'layoff readiness pack' (offboarding checklist, manager scripts, fund terms) and pitch 15 mid-size companies through two PEOs and an HR consultancy. Line up two training providers and one career-coaching group. Target letters of intent from 5-10 founding employers covering about 5,000 employees at roughly $15 per employee per month, with a first paying pool by month 3.

title: Independent Accuracy Certification for Wearable Health Claims
one_liner: A third-party lab that certifies wearable metrics (HRV, sleep staging, BP trends) now that the FDA has stepped back, funded by makers and trusted by buyers.
customer: Wearable and health-app makers selling into employers, payers, clinics, coaches and gyms (they pay for certification). Secondary: self-insured employers, payers and coaching platforms that subscribe to procurement-grade reports.
problem: Insiders cheered the FDA's January 2026 General Wellness guidance as freedom. But no clearance means no trusted filter: buyers cannot tell which of dozens of rings, watches and patches are accurate, one analysis argued wearables 'beat the FDA and lost the insurance money', and makers have no credible third-party proof to show payers. Claims exposure to the FTC, state AGs and class actions rises at the same time.
solution: Run a standing panel of about 200 volunteers with lab-grade references (ECG chest strap, a partner polysomnography lab, clinical and ambulatory BP, VO2/lactate testing). Test devices and features under a published protocol, issue tiered 'Verified for [metric]' marks with stated error bands (re-tested at major firmware changes), publish a public leaderboard, and sell buyers a procurement report they can cite in RFPs.
why_now: FDA's Jan 2026 wellness guidance lets physiologic-metric features (HRV, SpO2, BP trends) skip review; Whoop's BP feature drew a July 2025 warning letter and a June 2026 closeout; the HIPRA consumer-health-data bill cleared Senate HELP 22-0 on July 30, 2026, so scrutiny of wearable data is rising while the FDA filter is gone.
revenue_model: Certification fees of $15-60k per device or feature per year with re-test fees; $5-25k/yr buyer subscriptions for procurement reports; per-test fees for startups needing payer credibility.
non_obvious_insight: Deregulation does not remove the need for a trust filter, it privatizes it. The certifier is paid by makers but its only currency is buyer trust, so it must publish unflattering results (Consumer Reports crossed with a safety-lab model). Whoever writes the reference protocol first gets cited in payer and employer RFPs, which is a durable moat.
first_30_days: Partner with a university exercise-physiology or sleep lab, recruit 40 volunteers, test 6 popular rings/watches on resting HR, HRV and sleep staging against ECG/PSG, publish the methodology and preliminary results, then sell 2-3 employer-facing wearable startups a paid $15k pre-publication verification.

title: Boundary Truth: Ledger of Special-District Lines
one_liner: Turn recorded annexation, inclusion and exclusion instruments into a single authoritative boundary ledger that catches wrong tax bills, wrong ballots and wrong 911 routing.
customer: County assessors and treasurers, election offices, state 911 boards and NG911 GIS coordinators, plus special-district management firms and metro-district law firms. Paid through the recorder's technology or preservation fund (spendable at the recorder's discretion in many states), election grant money or 911 fee funds.
problem: There are about 39,000 special districts (fire, water, library, mosquito, metro) and their boundary changes are recorded with the county clerk as ministerial filings with no downstream notification. Nobody reliably updates the assessor's tax-area codes, the election office's address-to-district crosswalk or the 911 emergency-service boundary layer. Result: parcels billed by the wrong district or by none (lost revenue, later refunds), voters handed the wrong ballot style, and dispatch mismatches. State attorneys general have issued opinions on tax levies made after officials weren't notified of boundary changes. We discover the errors in the last two weeks before an election or when a taxpayer complains.
solution: An AI pipeline reads the recorded instruments (metes-and-bounds text, plats, ordinances), draws polygons with closure and area sanity checks, and routes low-confidence ones to a human reviewer. It keeps a versioned, effective-dated ledger of each district's legal boundary. It then diffs the ledger against the assessor's tax-area file, the voter address crosswalk and the 911 boundary layer, and returns a plain exception list such as '312 parcels inside Fire District 4 per the 2022 recorded inclusion but billed to no district.' Sell a fixed-price audit first, then an annual subscription.
why_now: Mid-decade redistricting fights and the 2026 midterms have made ballot-style accuracy politically radioactive. NG911 requires clean authoritative boundary GIS data. Property tax scrutiny makes every misbilled dollar a headline. LLMs can now parse legal descriptions well enough to draft polygons that a human reviews rather than draws.
revenue_model: $15k-$40k one-time boundary drift audit per county, then $10k-$30k/year per county for continuous monitoring, sized to fit inside a recorder's technology fund or a 911 board budget. Data-quality add-ons for district management firms and bond counsel.
non_obvious_insight: The legal boundary is the recorded instrument, not the GIS layer; the layer is just someone's drawing of a PDF. Because the clerk often sits at the junction of records, elections and sometimes tax, we see the stale cascade that assessors, election staff and 911 GIS analysts each see only a slice of. Also, the clerk's tech fund often sits outside the commissioners' budget fight, so a $25k audit can be approved in weeks, not the 18 months that scares govtech investors.
first_30_days: Pick one state heavy on special districts (Colorado metro districts, Texas MUDs and ESDs, Illinois, Washington, Florida CDDs). Offer a free boundary drift audit to a single county's assessor and clerk using five years of recorded inclusions and annexations. Turn the mismatch list into a paid pilot funded from the recorder's fund, then take the proof to the state 911 board.

title: Church-Basement Microschools for Retired Teachers
one_liner: A turnkey venue, insurance, fire-code and ESA-billing kit that lets a retired teacher open an 8-15 student paid school in a congregation's empty weekday classrooms.
customer: Retired or soon-to-retire teachers aged 55-70 pay a monthly fee and a share of tuition. Congregations are the landlords. Parents are the end payers, through education savings account (ESA) funds.
problem: Microschool builders assume curriculum and tech are the hard part. What actually kills these schools is the certificate of occupancy and zoning, the fire marshal, liability insurance, ESA vendor approval and reimbursement paperwork, and bookkeeping. Retired teachers have the credibility and skills but no business experience. Meanwhile congregations hold Sunday-school classrooms that sit empty Monday to Friday and need rent.
solution: A state-by-state permit packet (occupancy class, what the inspector will actually ask for). A pre-negotiated group liability policy for microschools. A standard five-day lease with congregations covering rent, cleaning, security and safeguarding. Onboarding for ESA and voucher programs (including any accreditation or approved-provider requirements) plus back-office billing and attendance. A menu of curricula so the teacher chooses. A shared bench of substitute retired teachers for sick days.
why_now: Texas launched its Education Freedom Accounts in fall 2026 with $1 billion, about $10,474 per student in 2026-27 (a 12-student school is roughly $125k in revenue), and about 600 private schools and pre-K providers applied in the first 10 days. Universal or near-universal ESAs are live in a growing list of states, and a federal scholarship tax credit begins in 2027. About 1.5 million students are already in microschools, and teacher retirements are climbing.
revenue_model: $199-$399/month platform fee per school, about 4% of tuition processed, insurance commissions, and a 5% lease-admin fee from congregations.
non_obvious_insight: Pension re-employment caps generally bite when you return to a covered public district. Working for yourself in a private school usually does not touch your annuity (verify by state), and past full retirement age the Social Security earnings test no longer applies. So a retired teacher can keep her pension and collect full tuition. Parents' top trust signal is 'Mrs. Alvarez taught 31 years at Lincoln Elementary.' A church building that is already zoned, already inspected for children, and rents for $800-$1,500 a month is the cost moat. Curriculum is commodity. Occupancy and insurance are the moat.
first_30_days: In Texas or Arizona or Florida, recruit a cohort of 10 retired teachers through retired-educator associations and Facebook groups. Line up 5 congregations with weekday space. Build the permit checklist for one city, get one group insurance quote, and sign 3 pilot schools at $299/month. Target the January 2027 semester and the early-2027 ESA application cycle for 2027-28, since fall 2026 enrollment has already closed.

title: Dark-Core Muscle Clinics in Converting Offices
one_liner: A plug-in metabolic and muscle clinic sized for the windowless middle of deep office floor plates that developers cannot turn into apartments, so dead space earns rent and GLP-1 users get an in-building place to keep their muscle.
customer: Office-to-residential developers and their lenders with deep-floorplate buildings (they gain a rent line on unusable area). Demand side: GLP-1 users who live or work in the building, plus employers that dropped GLP-1 coverage (employer coverage fell from 72% to 60% in 2026) and want a capped-cost program.
problem: Conversions only pencil when every bedroom can have a window, so deep floor plates lose a large share of each floor to unrentable middle or need expensive light wells. Meanwhile only about a third of non-diabetic GLP-1 patients persist at 1 year, stoppers regain weight roughly 4x faster than behavioral losers, and muscle loss is unmanaged. Nobody is paid to run a supervised strength-and-nutrition protocol close to where patients live and work.
solution: A standardized 3,000-6,000 sf module: body-composition scan, 6-8 supervised strength stations, dietitian rooms, lab draw, telehealth booths and pill-pickup lockers, run by a prescriber-agnostic clinical group so members can bring a Wegovy or Foundayo script from anywhere. Ambulatory clinics are Group B occupancy like offices, so no change of use is needed. Developers get a 'core-fill' master lease (low $/sf plus a slice of membership revenue) that improves conversion math and gives lenders a credit-tested income line. Members pay about $99/mo. Employers pay a capped per-employee fee.
why_now: The Wegovy pill (Jan 2026) and Lilly's Foundayo (Apr 2026) at about $149/mo turned GLP-1s into a mass cash-pay product, so millions of stop-and-restart cycles are coming. Employers are dropping coverage. Office vacancy is 17.8% with $289B of office loans maturing by 2028 and CMBS delinquency at 13.2%, so owners will trade rent for feasibility. Neko Health's $700M raise for a NYC launch shows urban demand for preventive scanning, yet nobody runs the muscle-and-adherence loop after the scan.
revenue_model: Memberships at $79-149/mo; per-member fees from employers and Medicare Advantage plans; body-comp and lab add-ons; a low-rent master lease with revenue share to the landlord.
non_obvious_insight: The thing that kills conversions (no daylight) is the one thing a clinic does not need. Because clinics share office occupancy class, the space is code-legal without a change of use. A clinic inside the building where hundreds of residents and lunch-hour office workers already are may be the highest-adherence location possible for a persistence problem.
first_30_days: Lease one vacant interior suite in a half-empty Class B office at near-zero rent with landlord-funded build-out. Open a 10-week 'GLP-1 muscle lab' with one exercise physiologist, a $10-15K body-composition scanner and a contracted dietitian. Sell 40-60 memberships to workers in the building and 2-3 local employers that dropped coverage. Take the adherence data to conversion developers with deep-plate buildings and sign 1-2 letters of intent.

title: Closing Ceremonies for Layoffs and Team Sunsets
one_liner: Trained ex-chaplains and celebrants who design and run dignified endings for teams hit by AI-driven layoffs, project sunsets and site closures.
customer: HR and people leaders at mid-size and large firms (500-5,000 employees) restructuring around AI, and outplacement firms that want to bundle a meaning-making service.
problem: Challenger reports AI was cited in about 112,713 announced US job cuts through July 2026 (about 24% of all cuts) and has led all reasons for five straight months. Layoffs are still delivered in a 15-minute video call and followed by résumé workshops. Nobody marks what ended, so leavers feel discarded, survivors feel guilty and disengage, and the company inherits hostile alumni.
solution: A 'Closing' package after legal communications are done: a facilitated last-day ceremony with a witness circle, a symbolic hand-off of work, a leaver-alumni charter (references, introductions), a manager script that bans corporate euphemism, and a survivor circle a week later. It is delivered in person or on video by a trained celebrant or ex-chaplain.
why_now: AI-attributed layoffs have become the leading cause of job cuts in 2026, and waves are recurring. Employer brand and alumni networks now matter for boomerang hiring and recruiting, and workers are openly sceptical of 'AI restructuring' messaging.
revenue_model: $4-12k per event, annual retainers of roughly $30-100k for an 'endings desk' that supports repeated restructurings, per-seat training licences for managers, and channel fees from outplacement partners.
non_obvious_insight: Companies overspend on what people do next and underspend on acknowledging what just ended. A layoff is a funeral without a ritual, and the missing ritual is the root of downstream problems: regretted attrition, employer-brand damage and lost referrals. A ceremony costs a tiny fraction of severance and is the only lever that changes how people talk about the company afterwards.
first_30_days: Recruit three ex-chaplains or celebrants. Build a 2-hour and a half-day format with a legal-review partner. Approach 15 outplacement consultants and 30 people-operations leaders, and offer one discounted team pilot in exchange for a case study.

title: Sunset Software Co: Pledge-Funded Tool Revival
one_liner: When a B2B tool announces its shutdown, customers pre-commit to paid 'extended life' contracts, and a small operator takes over only if a threshold is met.
customer: Companies stranded when a small dev or data tool shuts down or is acqui-hired away: CI runners, SQL clients, project trackers, metrics services. The founder of the dying tool is the second counterparty and receives a revenue share.
problem: Acqui-hires and product-gap closures strand paying customers with 30-90 days notice. BuildJet closed runners on 31 Mar 2026 because 'GitHub has made substantial improvements.' Cirrus CI closed on 1 Jun 2026 when Cirrus Labs joined OpenAI. Garnix shut down after being acquired. One customer wrote 'I have two CI providers to replace by the end of the Quarter.' Founders cannot sell the code. An Ask HN founder 'couldn't sell the codebase', and a commenter said 'no one wants some abandoned open source project for a defunct business.' PopSQL, SeekWell and Pivotal Tracker left solo builders racing to fill the gap.
solution: Run a 'continuity pledge' during the notice window. The customer signs a 12-month extended-life contract at 1.2-1.5x the old price, conditional on the operator reaching a minimum pledge total, like a Kickstarter for revival. If the threshold is met, the operator takes a code and brand licence, keeps the service running with a founder retainer or revenue share, and gets paid from day one. If not, nobody pays and nothing is bought. Portfolio economics do the rest: many small tools, shared infrastructure, no CAC.
why_now: AI-lab and platform acqui-hires now regularly turn small devtools into shutdown notices. Cirrus Labs joined OpenAI, Bun joined Anthropic, Astro joined Cloudflare, and Tailwind joined Shopify in the last year. The acquirer wants the team, not the customers. Permissive licences (Cirrus relicensed Tart and related tools as 'more permissive') make forks legal. The SimpleClosure H1 2026 report shows shutdowns running at scale.
revenue_model: 60-80% of extended-life fees kept by the operator, with 20-40% shared with the founder for 12 months. Later, cross-sell hosted plans to the open-source user base.
non_obvious_insight: A dying tool's code has no buyers, but its running service has customers who will pay. The sellable asset is customer continuity, and the pledge threshold removes the risk of buying dead code. Evidence: the Ask HN thread has a founder who could not sell his codebase and a commenter saying no one wants an abandoned project (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44398065). Cirrus CI's closure and Tart relicensing are covered at https://cirruslabs.org/ (HN discussion 47730194, 282 points). The Garnix thread has the 'two CI providers to replace by the end of the Quarter' comment (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48317043). BuildJet's notice sets the 31 Mar 2026 date (https://buildjet.com/for-github-actions/blog/we-are-shutting-down). Demand for a replacement shows up as solo builders rushing in, for example Saturn SQL after PopSQL and SeekWell (https://saturnsql.com) and the 10 teams racing to replace Pivotal Tracker (https://bye-tracker.net).
first_30_days: Week 1: set up a monitor on HN, status pages and changelogs for shutdown announcements. Week 2: pick one tool currently in its notice window and email the founder with a 12-month revenue-share offer. Weeks 3-4: publish a pledge page for that tool with a fixed pledge threshold and a 21-day deadline. If it clears the threshold, sign the licence and run the tool on shared infrastructure.

title: Lien-Release Chasing for Title Agents
one_liner: A per-release service that finds who now owns an old paid-off mortgage, sends the statutory demand, and chases the lender by voice, email and mail until the release is recorded.
customer: Independent title and escrow agencies and attorney closing offices, plus underwriters' curative departments. Priced per release delivered.
problem: An ALTA survey of 449 title professionals in 47 states (March 2026) found 59% name securing releases for prior mortgages as the most significant curative challenge. 60% of purchases need 3-5 title issues cleared before closing, over 90% involve mortgage payoffs, and 80%+ require reviewing at least 11 documents. HousingWire (September 25, 2026) reports search and exam is still mostly manual and files stall most on older or rural county records. A DataTrace study found generic public-record AI missed meaningful title matters in 40.8% of 200 searchable files, though that is a vendor study.
solution: Given a commitment with open-of-record mortgages, the system identifies the current holder or servicer from the chain of assignments, MERS servicer data and bank merger histories. It finds the right release department or statutory agent and sends a compliant satisfaction demand for that state. Voice agents work lender IVRs and phone queues, with email and certified-mail follow-up on a schedule. It monitors county recorder indexes and e-recording confirmations, uses lost-satisfaction affidavit routes where allowed, and posts a clear event back to the agent's title software. Human curative specialists take escalations such as executive letters to banks.
why_now: Title premiums hit $4.5B in Q1 2026 and volume rose nearly 14% in 2025, while ALTA says title costs fell about 5% even as operational demands and fraud work grew. Search-and-exam automation is crowded and improving (Qualia and others), which pushes the human bottleneck to the curative chase. Voice agents can now handle multi-turn calls with lender phone trees.
revenue_model: Fee per release delivered ($75-250 to test), success-only, plus a monthly minimum for agencies with steady volume. Upsell to underwriters as a curative-outsourcing vendor.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone is automating search and exam, but the survey says the hardest part is the human chase for releases, which is phone- and letter-heavy, statute-driven and rules-based, and has no dominant product. Most states set deadlines and penalties for lenders that fail to record satisfactions, so a correctly formatted demand gets a response (statute detail is my domain knowledge and needs verifying by state). Evidence: ALTA study (https://www.housingwire.com/articles/alta-study-title-production-complexity-curative-work/), the manual search-and-exam story (https://www.housingwire.com/articles/title-search-exam-manual/), and the AI-miss study (https://www.housingwire.com/articles/public-record-linked-ai-misses-key-title-issues-in-many-searches/).
first_30_days: Sign 3 title agencies as design partners with their first 20 releases free. Have them share historic release requests to seed a database of the top 200 servicers and bank-merger successors. Build demand templates for the 10 highest-volume states and a voice agent for the top lenders' release lines. Start charging per release by day 30 and log turnaround days versus the agency's manual baseline.

title: Battery-Islanded Feeders Instead of Undergrounding
one_liner: Sell utilities islandable rural feeders powered by enrolled home batteries as a cheaper alternative to undergrounding and repeated wildfire power shutoffs.
customer: Wildfire-exposed utilities and co-ops (California, Pacific Northwest, Colorado, Hawaii), funded from wildfire-mitigation capex. Tribal and community microgrids are a secondary buyer.
problem: Undergrounding costs roughly $2-3M or more per mile, and public safety power shutoffs cut power to thousands of homes for days. Home batteries are common (46% storage attach), but each only serves its own house, and utilities cannot use them to keep a whole feeder alive.
solution: A feeder-level controller, smart switch and grid-forming coordination software that lets a segment island when upstream is de-energized, with enrolled home batteries powering critical loads. The same software runs normal VPP dispatch to pay for itself. The utility contracts it as a non-wires wildfire alternative.
why_now: 140k batteries delivered 580 MW on Sept 9, grid-forming inverters are now standard, wildfire budgets are large, and affordability limits undergrounding.
revenue_model: $150-400 per customer-year availability payment from the utility, a controller lease, and VPP revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: The battery is already in the house, and the missing pieces are coordination and a switch. Utilities cannot earn a return on efficiency, but they can on wildfire mitigation capex, and you are competing against $3M per mile.
first_30_days: Approach small co-ops and munis in fire-prone areas. Pick a 200-home feeder with at least 30% battery attach. Propose a paid $40k feasibility study and a pilot using existing devices. Partner with a microgrid-controller vendor.

title: Foreign-Ties Clearance Pack for SBIR Startups
one_liner: A fixed-price, agency-ready foreign-involvement and cyber-readiness dossier priced to fit inside the SBIR technical-assistance allowance, so the startup pays nothing out of pocket.
customer: SBIR/STTR Phase I and Phase II applicants and awardees (DoD, DOE, NSF, NIH, EPA). Secondary buyers are seed and VC funds with SBIR-heavy portfolios that need LP-level attestations for their companies.
problem: The Small Business Innovation and Economic Security Act (S. 3971, signed April 13, 2026, extends SBIR/STTR through FY2031) makes agencies run risk-based due diligence on every applicant. The review covers foreign ownership and financial ties, foreign affiliations of key personnel, licensing deals and joint ventures, and links to the UFLPA, Chinese Military-Industrial Complex, Commerce Entity and Section 889 lists. It also covers cybersecurity practices, patent analysis and employee analysis. Applicants must file disclosures. A 4-person startup has no idea what an agency will find in its cap table (LPs behind the VC funds), co-inventors, or contractors. Agencies may notify of a denial only 'as appropriate', so a rejection may come with no explanation.
solution: A software-plus-analyst service that ingests the cap table, team list, patents and vendor list. It does look-through on investors (SEC Form ADV and Form D, GLEIF, OpenCorporates). It screens every name against the free BIS Consolidated Screening List and the UFLPA and CMIC lists. It checks co-inventor and employee affiliations (USPTO PatentsView, ORCID) and takes a NIST 800-171/SPRS cyber baseline. Output is a disclosure-ready packet, a red-flag remediation memo (for example 'restructure this side letter'), and a yearly re-screen. Sold as a vendor the awardee can pick for technical and business assistance (T&BA) money.
why_now: S. 3971 was signed April 13, 2026. The T&BA allowance was raised to $6,500 per Phase I and $50,000 per Phase II, and it now explicitly covers 'cybersecurity assistance' and 'screening for potential foreign involvement'. The lapse from October 2025 to April 2026 created a backlog: DOE alone opened about $147M of FY25 Phase II on July 22, 2026, and the FY26 Genesis Mission Phase I is open. Every awardee now faces the new diligence for the first time.
revenue_model: $2,500 to $6,500 flat per Phase I (fits under the $6,500 T&BA cap, so it is free to the founder). $15k to $50k per Phase II package. $1,200 per year for a re-screen subscription when the cap table changes. VC portfolio bundles at $500 to $1,000 per company.
non_obvious_insight: Congress created an earmarked wallet for exactly this service, and the buyer has zero price sensitivity because the money can't be spent on anything else. S. 3971 Section 7 amends Section 9(q) to allow T&BA funds for 'cybersecurity assistance' and 'screening for potential foreign involvement', up to $6,500 (Phase I) and $50,000 (Phase II) per project, and lets recipients choose their own vendors. Section 2 (new Section 9(vv)) lists the diligence factors agencies must assess (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119s3971enr/html/BILLS-119s3971enr.htm). DOE confirms the April 13, 2026 signing, extension through FY2031, new security due-diligence mandates, and the reopened Phase II money (https://www.energy.gov/technologycommercialization/doe-small-business-innovation-research-sbir-and-small-business). The hard part is not screening names but LP-level look-through on venture funds, which is opaque and which no compliance vendor packages for a 4-person startup. Caveat: I could not confirm which agencies have opened T&BA vendor lists yet, so check that first.
first_30_days: Week 1: build a free 'SBIR foreign-risk self-check' web tool on top of the BIS Consolidated Screening List API and the UFLPA list. Use it as the lead magnet. Weeks 1 to 2: pull the last 12 months of Phase I/II awardees from the public SBIR.gov awards data and email 300 founders quoting the exact statute language. Weeks 2 to 4: manually produce 5 free dossiers for design partners to learn where the LP look-through breaks. Ask each agency SBIR office (start with DOE OTC, NSF and Navy) how to be listed as a T&BA vendor. Close 5 paid packs at $2.5k to $6.5k.

title: Two-Way Kasuhara Desk for Tiny Japanese Businesses
one_liner: A QR-and-LINE 'complaint lane' plus staff backup button that gives micro-businesses the customer-harassment policy, consultation channel and evidence log Japan now requires.
customer: Owners of Japanese businesses with 1-100 employees that face customers in person (izakaya, clinics, salons, cram schools, taxi and care operators, retail). They pay ¥2,980-9,800 per site per month. Resale channels are sharoushi (labor and social-insurance consultants) and SME insurance agents.
problem: From 1 Oct 2026 every Japanese employer with at least one employee must publish a policy against customer harassment ('kasuhara'), set up and publicize a consultation channel, and have response procedures. There is no phase-in. Most tiny firms have no HR function, no policy and no channel. Staff also hesitate to report incidents. Customers, for their part, now hesitate to voice legitimate complaints.
solution: (1) A QR code at the counter, on receipts and on LINE opens a structured, polite complaint form (what happened, photo, desired resolution). The owner gets a timestamped record, and abusive or threatening messages are flagged. (2) A 'need backup' button in LINE gives frontline staff an anonymous route to a partner sharoushi or counselor. That route is the required consultation channel. (3) A one-tap incident log that creates a dated evidence pack (notes, optional call-recording notice, response taken). (4) A policy, poster and work-rule addendum generator that meets the MHLW guideline. (5) A monthly 'compliance proof' PDF for the day the labor bureau asks.
why_now: The MHLW guideline was published on 26 Feb 2026 and the duty takes effect 1 Oct 2026, three days from today. Incumbent tooling targets call centers, such as SoftBank's SoftVoice AI voice-softener launched Feb 2026. Nothing is priced or packaged for a 5-person restaurant. The Oct 1 news cycle will also push owners to search for a fix.
revenue_model: ¥2,980/month per site (¥9,800 for 10+ staff), ¥30,000 optional setup for work-rule revision, and a 30% recurring rev-share to sharoushi and insurance agents who resell it. A later upsell is per-incident counselor escalation. Insurers may white-label it into SME liability packages.
non_obvious_insight: The law has a hidden chilling effect on the customer side. In the Channel Corporation survey (497 customer-facing employees plus 514 consumers, June 2026), 52.3% of consumers who hit a store error 'let it pass' for fear of being labelled a harasser, and 65.2% wanted AI-mediated ways to raise issues. A product that gives customers a legitimate complaint lane defuses harassment at the source and doubles as the mandatory paper trail. Enforcement is guidance and then naming rather than fines, so buyers want the cheapest defensible record, not AI detection. Only under 10% of firms use technical measures. Evidence: KiteRa survey of 965 workers on 10-11 Sep 2026 found 61.3% with no policy, 68.3% with no publicized channel, 58.6% of firms with 100 or fewer employees with no channel at all, and 19.8% of workers harassed in the past year, of whom 74.9% hesitated to report (https://prtimes.jp/main/html/rd/p/000000130.000045846.html). Channel Corp found 51.7% with no measures at all (https://ecnomikata.com/ecnews/customerservice/51126/). Legal scope and enforcement: https://www.twobirds.com/en/insights/2026/singapore/customer-harassment-prevention-now-a-statutory-obligation-for-employers-in-japan. Incumbent focus on call centers: https://www.softbank.jp/en/sbnews/entry/20260219_01.
first_30_days: Days 1-3: Ship a free policy-and-poster generator plus a LINE Official Account to catch Oct 1 search traffic, and a landing page in Japanese. Days 4-14: Recruit 5-10 sharoushi (offer 30% recurring share and a white-label report) and 2 local shokokai chambers; sell 'compliance by Friday' to their existing clients. Build the QR complaint form with LINE Messaging API (no app needed) and manually route staff-backup messages to one partner counselor. Days 15-30: Sign 30-50 shops at ¥2,980 and collect 3 named case studies. Ask an SME insurance agency to pilot a bundled offer.

title: Exit Ramps for Dying AI Platforms
one_liner: A converter plus fixed-price migration service that turns Flowise flows, OpenAI Agent Builder graphs and Assistants API integrations into portable, regression-tested code.
customer: AI automation agencies that have 5-50 client agents built on Flowise, Agent Builder or the Assistants API, and in-house AI teams at SMEs that have no engineer to spare. They pay per migrated agent.
problem: Three AI platforms are being killed within about 90 days. The Assistants API shut down on 26 Aug 2026. Agent Builder shuts down on 30 Nov 2026. Flowise was archived in mid-Aug 2026 and its core team leaves on 31 Aug. Non-technical teams built visual flows they cannot maintain as raw code. A Flowise insider says forkers 'own dependency updates, security patches, and model API churn indefinitely, and the contributor community that used to absorb that work is dispersing.' A commenter says telling non-engineers to maintain a TypeScript codebase 'is not a real answer.'
solution: Build importers for Flowise chatflow JSON, Agent Builder workflow exports and Assistants objects (assistants, threads, vector stores, files). They feed a neutral intermediate representation. Exporters then emit (a) Agents SDK / Responses API code, (b) n8n workflows, (c) Langflow. The differentiator is a parity proof. Historical conversation logs are replayed against old and new stacks, and the agency receives a behavioral-diff report it can send to its client. The output is plain, readable code that a coding agent such as Claude Code can maintain. Flowise itself says developers are moving to coding agents because 'rigid workflow low code approach quickly hits the limit.'
why_now: The Assistants API shutdown (26 Aug 2026), the Agent Builder deadline (30 Nov 2026) and the Flowise archive (Aug 2026) all land in one quarter, which forces spending on a real deadline. Coding agents now make code-first output maintainable by non-experts. Flowise has 55.5k stars and 25k forks, so the stranded installed base is large.
revenue_model: Fixed-price migration of $500-2,500 per agent. An agency plan of $199/mo keeps flows mirrored in the intermediate representation with a nightly 'can I still leave?' test. The free converter CLI is the lead magnet.
non_obvious_insight: The demand is a deadline plus a maintenance gap, not a tooling gap. Evidence: OpenAI's deprecations page gives the Agent Builder shutdown as 30 Nov 2026 and the Assistants API as 26 Aug 2026 (https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/deprecations). Flowise's sunset notice sets the code freeze, the archive and the end of core-team support (https://flowiseai.com/sunset). The GitHub repo shows 55.5k stars, 25k forks and 699 open issues (https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise). The HN thread quotes the 'not a real answer' complaint and notes that OpenAI's own Agent Builder is also going away (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49176920). Agencies that resell agents to clients are the buyers, and they carry portfolio risk that a single hobbyist does not. The parity report is what they sell on to their clients.
first_30_days: Week 1: mine the Flowise Discord, GitHub issues and r/n8n for stranded users. Ship a free 'flowise-to-n8n / Agents SDK' CLI that handles the 3 most common node types. Weeks 2-3: cold-DM 40 agencies and sell 5-10 pilot migrations at $750, prioritizing Agent Builder users before the 30 Nov deadline. Week 4: turn the manual steps in those migrations into automated exporters and publish before/after parity reports as case studies.

title: Royalty-Exact Generators: One Adapter per Creator
one_liner: A generative sound-effects and sample tool where every contributor has their own adapter, so payouts are exact by construction instead of guessed after the fact.
customer: Indie game developers, video editors and YouTubers buying sound effects and samples (paying users), with foley artists and sample-pack producers as the opt-in supply side.
problem: Attribution in generative AI is post-hoc guesswork: the Spotify-UMG covers deal promises credit and compensation but discloses no tracking method. Small creators are excluded from label-scale licensing deals. Buyers want output they can use commercially without a legal cloud.
solution: Fine-tune a small open text-to-audio model with a separate adapter per consenting creator. Each generation composes adapters with explicit weights, and royalties follow those weights, so attribution is bookkeeping rather than research. Every output carries a watermark and a per-generation receipt. Start with short sound effects and foley, where inference is cheap, demand is high and buyers' licensing needs are simple.
why_now: Adapter fine-tuning is cheap, Suno's Sep 9 switch to licensed training shows licensed models are becoming the norm, and the credit-and-compensation gap in the Spotify-UMG deal is visible.
revenue_model: $15-50/month subscriptions plus usage credits, with 60-70% distributed to adapter owners pro rata, and enterprise indemnified licenses for studios.
non_obvious_insight: Attribution research tries to recover influence from a monolithic model. Changing the architecture turns attribution into accounting, and small, narrow, licensed models beat large generic ones on legal risk.
first_30_days: Recruit 30 foley artists and sample makers via forums and Gumroad and itch.io sellers. Fine-tune adapters on an open SFX model, demo composite generations with receipts, and pre-sell $99 annual plans to 100 indie developers via itch.io and Discord.

title: Glasses-Free Zone: Smart-Glasses Detection Kits
one_liner: A detection-plus-policy kit for rooms where camera glasses cannot be allowed (exam centers, courtrooms, medical rooms, locker rooms, poker rooms), with logged, defensible procedures.
customer: Independent test centers, licensing and language-test operators, court administrators, casinos and poker rooms, med-spas, therapy and medical offices, gyms and locker-room operators.
problem: Camera and AI glasses look like ordinary eyewear and are now cheap and everywhere. Venues have bans on paper but no way to enforce or prove violations. In May 2026 two TOEIC test-takers were caught with AI glasses and banned for four years. The College Board banned smart glasses (even prescription ones) at the SAT starting March 2026, and New York State courts banned them across all courthouses in 2026.
solution: A door-frame or desk unit combining Bluetooth and Wi-Fi signature scanning for known glasses families, plus an optional optical check for camera lenses. It ships with a written policy pack, non-accusatory staff scripts, signage, a tamper-evident event log usable in score-invalidation or eviction disputes, and a short staff certification. The software updates as new glasses launch.
why_now: Camera-and-AI glasses went mainstream in 2025 to 2026, and other brands are launching. Institutions responded with bans in months, but incumbents (exam vendors, courts, gyms) have no tooling or procedures. The 18-month gap is between glasses in millions of faces and venue-grade controls. Consumer detector apps exist, but no one owns the evidence-grade, staff-friendly layer.
revenue_model: $299 to $999 policy and training kit, $1,500 to $5,000 per site for hardware install, then $49 to $149 per month for signature updates, incident logging and re-certification.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer's problem isn't detection accuracy, it's defensibility. A test center that cancels a score or a court that ejects a spectator needs a repeatable, logged, non-accusatory process to survive an appeal or a complaint. Sell the paper trail and the staff script, and treat the sensor as an accessory. False accusations, not misses, are what scare institutions.
first_30_days: Build a prototype scanner on an ESP32 or Raspberry Pi with known Bluetooth signatures from Ray-Ban Meta and other glasses, and test on real devices. Write the policy kit with an ex-proctor or court-security advisor. Offer paid pilots to 10 independent test-prep and test centers, one poker room and two med-spas. Charge for the kit from the start.

title: Federal-Equipment Disposition Desk for Closing Labs
one_liner: A compliance-plus-resale service that clears federal-interest, decontaminates and re-homes grant-funded instruments when labs shrink or close.
customer: University research-administration and property offices, independent research institutes, SBIR-funded startups winding down, and the roughly 300 'zombie' biotechs Owl Posting counts.
problem: Instruments bought with federal funds carry federal-interest and disposition rules (2 CFR 200.313, with a per-unit threshold), which stall resale. Freezers, cryostats and sequencers sit idle or get trashed. NIH grant terminations, 15,000+ biopharma job cuts and 50+ shrinking companies add supply, while small labs cannot afford new equipment. The brief flags used-equipment liquidation for squeezed labs as an underserved gap.
solution: An asset-level 'federal-interest passport': identify the award and agency, determine the obligation, prepare disposition requests and valuation, arrange decontamination certificates, pack and ship, and list to vetted buyers. Commission plus compliance fee.
why_now: Funding turbulence and layoffs are producing lab closures now, and marketplaces for used equipment exist but do not solve permission or liability.
revenue_model: 15-25% commission on resale, $500-2,500 per-asset compliance fees, and institutional annual retainers.
non_obvious_insight: The seller's pain is permission and liability, not price discovery, so marketplaces do not fix it. The compliance passport is the unlock, and attaching one at purchase time makes instruments 'resale-ready' and turns the desk into a recurring service.
first_30_days: Contact 10 mid-tier university property or research-admin offices and 30 winding-down SBIR startups. Process 5 pilot disposals. Template the passport. Partner with a decontamination and shipping vendor.

title: WhatsApp Voice-Note Superintendent for Spec Builders
one_liner: A bilingual coordinator-plus-AI service that runs daily crew confirmations, headcounts and re-sequencing for a builder's two dozen subs over WhatsApp voice notes, priced per house.
customer: Small private and spec builders (20-300 homes a year) in Texas, Florida and the Southeast, and remodelers who juggle many subs.
problem: A typical home needs about two dozen subs. Foundations sit 30+ days waiting for crews, and one executive described 15-20 houses stuck 6+ weeks. Builders learn a crew is not coming days too late. Project software requires English typing and logins, and workers are wary of anything that looks like tracking. Procore's 20 agents serve larger GCs.
solution: Foremen keep sending Spanish voice notes on WhatsApp. The system transcribes them, extracts headcount, phase status and photos, and updates the schedule. A nearshore bilingual coordinator confirms tomorrow's crews by 5 p.m., calls backup crews when there is a gap, and sends the builder one exception report each morning. Privacy by design: counts and progress only, no IDs or location.
why_now: ICE arrests rose from 32,545 in May to 49,571 in July 2026. Crews can shrink overnight (a Minnesota roofing crew went from 80 to 6). Multilingual speech models and the WhatsApp Business API are mature, and PM incumbents are focused on big GCs.
revenue_model: $300-500 per active house per month, or $3-6K per month per builder. One coordinator handles 25-40 houses, so gross margin is high.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not scheduling math, it is that the people who know whether tomorrow's crew is coming do not use the software. The interface must be the phone and language they already use. The daily headcount is the leading indicator, and knowing a day earlier lets a builder re-sequence trades instead of idling a foundation.
first_30_days: Sign 3 builders with 10-20 active houses each through a home builders association. Hire one bilingual coordinator. Run it manually with WhatsApp and a shared sheet, add speech-to-text in week 2, and document five saved crew-days.

title: Mindbody Escape Hatch: Studio Migration Concierge
one_liner: A flat-fee service that moves a studio's members, class packs and payment tokens off Mindbody without losing revenue.
customer: Boutique studios, gyms, yoga and Pilates operators on Mindbody (about 40,000 businesses) paying $159-699 per month plus marketplace commissions.
problem: After the ClassPass/Mindbody/EGYM combination (a $7.5B deal completed in 2026), owners report about 23.5 percent effective marketplace commissions and a roughly $500 data-export fee on cancellation. Lock-in is not the software but the card-on-file payment tokens and member history, so owners fear migration will churn members.
solution: A fixed-fee migration ($1.5-3k): export clients, attendance, waivers, packs and memberships; execute PCI-compliant processor-to-processor token migration; map intro offers and unlimited plans; rebuild schedule widgets; run parallel billing checks; and message members by SMS. Target alternative platforms pay a bounty per migrated studio.
why_now: Consolidation gave studios a reason to re-evaluate, ClassPass is rolling out studio-friendly policies in response to complaints, and processors now support token migration.
revenue_model: $1.5-3k per migration plus $200-400 bounty per studio from the receiving software vendor and an optional $99 per month retention audit.
non_obvious_insight: The moat is edge-case knowledge (paused members, unlimited plans, refunds, tokens), not software, and rival vendors will pay you for customers because their own acquisition cost is high.
first_30_days: Offer five free migration audits in studio-owner communities, pick two target platforms, run three at-cost pilot migrations, and turn the playbook into a checklist and pricing page.

title: Robot Access Passport for Commercial Buildings
one_liner: One certified robot identity, insurance certificate and elevator/door gateway that lets any delivery, cleaning or humanoid robot enter a building, with landlords collecting a fee.
customer: Owners and managers of office towers, multifamily REITs, hospitals, hotels and malls, who pay a subscription. Robot operators pay per-robot access fees.
problem: Every robot vendor negotiates separately with building management on elevator integration, insurance, liability and hours. Buildings have no policy or tooling, and incidents have no clear owner. This gets worse as sidewalk, cleaning, security and humanoid pilots multiply.
solution: A $1-2k building-side controller integrated with elevators, doors and turnstiles through existing vendor APIs or relays, plus a registry that verifies operator, insurance, firmware version and incident hotline. A policy engine sets quiet hours, zones and speed limits, with usage-based billing. Landlords earn a share of access fees, and robot operators integrate once for many buildings.
why_now: About 22k humanoids shipped in H1 2026, delivery robots and drones are moving to multifamily, and regulators (NHTSA's July 2026 first-responder letter) are pushing for accountability. Buildings are the next permission bottleneck.
revenue_model: $150-400 a month per building in SaaS plus $5-15 per robot per month in access fees, split with the landlord, and installation margin.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource in robot deployment is permission, and building owners are the gatekeepers with zero tooling. A neutral gatekeeper standard is a two-sided network, like 'ID.me plus a certificate of insurance for robots', and landlords get paid to adopt it.
first_30_days: Approach 2 property managers in one metro where delivery robots already operate. Build an integration for one elevator vendor's open API, get a certificate-of-insurance template from a broker, and charge $500 a month for the pilot.
